title: The first adhan
hookLine: a companion dreams the call to prayer, and Bilal, with the best voice, calls it

lines: A FIRE? A HORN? A CLAPPER?
cards: Medina has a mosque now, mud walls and palm pillars. But nobody has clocks. People are working in date groves, in the market, at home, and prayer time comes, and half of them miss it.
So the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions sit down to solve it. How do you call a whole town together, five times a day? Someone suggests lighting a fire.
Someone, a horn. Someone, striking a wooden clapper, the way their neighbors did. Nothing feels right.
Then one night, a man from Medina has a dream. And the answer isn't an instrument at all. It's a human voice.

teach.b: The man was Abdullah ibn Zayd.

In the hadith, in the collections of Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, he dreams of a man carrying a wooden clapper and asks to buy it, to call people to prayer. The man says: shall I show you something better?
And he teaches him the words. Allahu akbar, God is greater, four times. I bear witness there is no god but God.
I bear witness Muhammad is the messenger of God. Come to prayer. Come to success.
God is greater. There is no god but God. In the morning Abdullah runs to the Prophet, who says: it's a true dream.
Go and teach the words to Bilal; his voice carries further than yours. Then Umar hurries in: he dreamed the very same thing. Now, Bilal.

Bilal ibn Rabah was an Abyssinian, a black African man who had been enslaved in Mecca. When he became Muslim, his master tortured him in the desert heat, a heavy stone on his chest, to make him give it up.
The early biographers say he just kept repeating one word: ahad, ahad.
One, one. Abu Bakr bought his freedom. And now, in Medina, the Prophet chooses this man, formerly enslaved, from far away, to stand up and call the whole city to God.

It's often said he'd climb onto the highest roof near the mosque at dawn to call. Muslims have called him the first mu'adhdhin ever since, and every adhan anywhere in the world goes back to his voice.

how: The adhan is called before each of the five daily prayers, from mosques around the world, and many Muslims answer by repeating its words quietly as they hear them; Sunni and Shia adhans share most of their words, with some differences.

o: the spoken call that gathers people to prayer
a drum or horn sounded at prayer times
the prayer itself, said in rows at the mosque

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Prophet dreamed the adhan himself
a companion, Abdullah ibn Zayd, dreamed it, and Umar dreamed it too.
Bilal had been enslaved in Mecca
tortured for his faith, freed by Abu Bakr, and chosen to call the first adhan.
before the adhan, a horn or a clapper was considered
they discussed a fire, a horn and a wooden clapper before the dream.

games.q: the words of the call have come in a dream to Abdullah ibn Zayd. who should call them out to the city?
games.why: Bilal: go and teach him the words, the Prophet said, because his voice carries further than yours.

practice: If you can, find a recording of an adhan, from any mosque, any country, and listen all the way through; if not, imagine a single voice rising over rooftops before dawn, long notes, the same words for fourteen centuries.
Notice how it starts: God is greater, whatever you were doing, whatever you were worried about. Let the sound settle into the quiet after it.

wordCard.voice: Adhan, the call to prayer: taught in a dream to Abdullah ibn Zayd, and first called out by Bilal.

orig.note: Arabic: the call, the announcement. the one who calls is the mu'adhdhin.

carryVoice: Your line: bilal calls. First a dream in the night, then a voice over the rooftops. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 499; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 189 (Abdullah ibn Zayd's dream; teach it to Bilal)
Sahih al-Bukhari 604 (the discussion of how to call people to prayer)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham): Bilal's torture, 'ahad, ahad', freed by Abu Bakr
